## Why People Choose All-on-4 Dental Implants (It's Not the Price)

URL: https://www.renewimplants.ca/blog/why-people-are-choosing-all-on-4
Published: 2026-09-29
Updated: 2026-09-29
Query: why choose all-on-4 dental implants

Why adults in Ottawa and across Canada choose All-on-4 implants over dentures: fixed teeth, fewer implants, same-day results, and decades of clinical data.

Questions:

Q: Who usually gets All-on-4 dental implants?
A: Most people who choose All-on-4 are over 50 and have lost most of their teeth in one or both jaws, or have failing teeth and dentures that no longer fit. More people in their late 30s and 40s are now choosing it earlier instead of cycling through temporary fixes.

Q: How long do All-on-4 implants last?
A: In a long-term study of All-on-4 in the lower jaw, 99.2% of the fixed bridges were still in place after up to 10 years. A follow-up of 10 to 18 years reported 93% implant survival. Home care and regular check-ups matter as much as the surgery.

Q: Do I need bone grafting for All-on-4?
A: Often not. The two back implants are angled to reach denser bone toward the front of the jaw, which is one reason many people who were told they needed grafting can still be treated. A 3D scan at your consultation confirms what applies to you.

Q: Can I get teeth the same day with All-on-4?
A: In many cases, yes. When the implants are stable enough on surgery day, a temporary fixed bridge is attached before you go home. Your final bridge is made after the gums and bone heal.

## Dentures vs. Dental Implants: Which Is Right for You?

URL: https://www.renewimplants.ca/blog/dentures-vs-dental-implants
Published: 2026-09-29
Updated: 2026-09-29
Query: dentures vs dental implants

Compare dentures and dental implants side by side: stability, comfort, jawbone health, and daily care, so you know exactly what to ask at your free consultation.

Questions:

Q: Are dental implants better than dentures?
A: Implants are more stable and help preserve the jawbone, while conventional dentures are removable and rest on the gums. Which is better depends on your bone, gum health, budget, and preferences. Many denture wearers choose a middle path, such as snap-on dentures held by implants.

Q: Can I switch from dentures to implants?
A: Yes. Many of our patients have worn dentures for years before switching. A 3D scan shows how much bone you have and whether angled implants, like All-on-4, can avoid grafting.

Q: Does the Canadian Dental Care Plan cover implants?
A: CDCP covers complete and partial dentures and, with preauthorization, overdentures. It does not list most implant treatment as covered. Our team checks exactly what applies to you and explains your options at the consultation.

Q: Do dental implants hurt?
A: Most people feel some soreness and swelling for a few days after surgery, which usually improves as the mouth heals. Sedation options are available if you're nervous.

## Same-Day Dental Implants: Can You Get New Teeth in One Day?

URL: https://www.renewimplants.ca/blog/same-day-dental-implants-new-teeth-one-day
Published: 2026-09-29
Updated: 2026-09-29
Query: same day dental implants

How same-day dental implants work, who usually qualifies, what recovery feels like, and when a staged plan is safer. Plain-English answers from Renew Implants.

Questions:

Q: Can you really get dental implants in one day?
A: In many cases, yes. The implants are placed and a temporary fixed bridge is attached the same day, so you leave with a full set of teeth. The final bridge is made a few months later, after healing.

Q: Who is not a good candidate for same-day implants?
A: People with active gum disease, not enough bone to hold the implants firmly on day one, or other treatment needs may be better served by a staged plan. A 3D scan and exam at your consultation decide which approach is safer for you.

Q: What can I eat after same-day implants?
A: Soft foods for the first weeks while the implants bond with the bone. Your team will give you a food guide and tell you when you can return to a normal diet.

Q: Are same-day teeth permanent?
A: The same-day teeth are a temporary fixed bridge. After the implants have healed, they are replaced with your final bridge, designed and made in our onsite lab.

## All-on-4 After Years of Missing Teeth: Is It Too Late?

URL: https://www.renewimplants.ca/blog/all-on-4-dental-implants-after-years-of-missing-teeth
Published: 2026-09-29
Updated: 2026-09-29
Query: all on 4 after years of missing teeth

Missing teeth for 10 or 20 years? Learn what happens to your jawbone, how angled All-on-4 implants often avoid bone grafting, and who may be a good candidate.

Questions:

Q: Is it too late for implants if I've had no teeth for years?
A: Not necessarily. Many people who lost their teeth 10 or 20 years ago can still get a fixed set of teeth. A 3D scan shows how much bone remains and which approach fits.

Q: What happens to the jawbone after teeth are lost?
A: The bone that held the teeth shrinks because it no longer gets pressure from chewing. A systematic review found the ridge can lose 29 to 63% of its width within about six months of an extraction, and the change continues more slowly after that.

Q: Will I need a bone graft?
A: Sometimes, but often not with All-on-4. The back implants are angled to reach denser bone at the front of the jaw. Your surgeon confirms this after the 3D scan.

Q: I've worn dentures for decades. Can I still switch?
A: Yes. Long-term denture wearers are some of our most common All-on-4 patients. The consultation checks your bone and gums and explains the options, including snap-on dentures.

## Full Arch vs. Individual Dental Implants: Key Differences

URL: https://www.renewimplants.ca/blog/full-arch-vs-individual-dental-implants
Published: 2026-09-29
Updated: 2026-09-29
Query: full arch vs individual dental implants

Individual implants replace single teeth; full arch implants replace a whole row on as few as four posts. Compare cases, treatment, and daily care side by side.

Questions:

Q: What is the difference between full arch and individual implants?
A: An individual implant replaces one tooth with one post and one crown. A full arch replaces an entire upper or lower row with a single bridge supported by several implants, often four.

Q: When is a full arch better than several single implants?
A: When most teeth in a jaw are missing or failing. Replacing each tooth separately would take many implants and more surgery, while a full arch restores the whole row on as few as four.

Q: Can I have a full arch on the top and dentures on the bottom?
A: Yes. Each jaw is planned on its own. Some patients start with one arch and add the other later, or pair a full arch with snap-on dentures.

## Does the Canadian Dental Care Plan Cover Dental Implants?

URL: https://www.renewimplants.ca/blog/does-the-canadian-dental-care-plan-cover-dental-implants
Published: 2026-10-14
Updated: 2026-10-14
Query: does cdcp cover dental implants

Does CDCP cover dental implants? The federal plan lists many dentures. Its benefits guide excludes implants and implant-supported dentures.

Short answer:

No. The Canadian Dental Care Plan does not cover dental implants. The Dental Benefits Guide excludes implants and all implant-related procedures, including dentures supported by implants, and says those exclusions are not eligible for reconsideration. Many removable dentures are listed separately, and some of them need preauthorization.

Key takeaways:

- The Dental Benefits Guide says it prevails when a shorter summary conflicts with it.
- Implants, implant crowns, bone grafts, and dentures supported by implants are named exclusions.
- Many removable dentures are listed, and some of them need preauthorization.
- A listed service can still be denied. Coverage is not automatic.

Questions:

Q: Does the Canadian Dental Care Plan pay for All-on-4?
A: The Dental Benefits Guide lists implants and all implant-related procedures as exclusions, including crowns supported by implants and dentures supported by implants. Those exclusions are not eligible for reconsideration. All-on-4 is implant treatment, so do not expect the plan to pay for it.

Q: Are overdentures covered?
A: The coverage page lists complete immediate and overdentures with preauthorization, and the guide's frequency table also lists complete overdentures with preauthorization. The same guide excludes complete and partial dentures supported by implants. A tooth-borne overdenture and an implant-supported denture are not the same thing.

Q: If a service is listed, is it approved?
A: No. The coverage page says the plan covers a portion of many services, some need preauthorization, and not every request is approved.

Sources:

- Canadian Dental Care Plan — What is covered (Government of Canada): https://www.canada.ca/en/services/benefits/dental/dental-care-plan/coverage.html
- Canadian Dental Care Plan — Dental Benefits Guide (Government of Canada): https://www.canada.ca/en/services/benefits/dental/dental-care-plan/guide.html

## Can You Get Dental Implants If You Have Bone Loss?

URL: https://www.renewimplants.ca/blog/dental-implants-with-bone-loss
Published: 2026-10-14
Updated: 2026-10-14
Query: dental implants with bone loss

Dental implants with bone loss are not an automatic no. A review measured ridge shrinkage after extraction, and All-on-4 was built around the bone that remains.

Short answer:

Bone loss does not automatically rule out dental implants. The jaw ridge shrinks after teeth are removed, especially in width during the first months. The All-on-4 concept was published as a way to use the bone that remains in an atrophic jaw. Whether that fits you is a scan question, not a slogan.

Key takeaways:

- After extraction, the jaw ridge loses more width than height in the first months.
- Tan and colleagues reported mean buccal losses of 3.79 mm horizontally and 1.24 mm vertically at six months.
- The All-on-4 concept was described as a way to use remnant bone and avoid regenerative procedures.
- That review also says the evidence is limited. A 3D scan is still required.

Questions:

Q: Does bone loss rule out dental implants?
A: Not by itself. The ridge does shrink after teeth are removed, but whether implants can be placed depends on the bone that remains, which a 3D scan shows. The All-on-4 concept was published as a way to use remnant bone in atrophic jaws.

Q: How fast does the jawbone shrink after an extraction?
A: A 2012 systematic review of human re-entry studies found rapid change in the first three to six months. Mean buccal reduction at six months was 3.79 mm horizontally and 1.24 mm vertically. Horizontal loss was reported as 29 to 63 percent and vertical loss as 11 to 22 percent around six months.

Q: Does All-on-4 avoid bone grafting?
A: The published concept was developed to use remnant bone and to avoid regenerative procedures, with two posterior implants angled to shorten the cantilever. The same review says the evidence is limited by sample size, follow-up, and attrition. It is not a promise that grafting is never needed.

Sources:

- A systematic review of post-extractional alveolar hard and soft tissue dimensional changes in humans (Clinical Oral Implants Research): https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22211303/
- The all-on-four treatment concept: Systematic review (Journal of Clinical and Experimental Dentistry): https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5347302/

## Snap-On Dentures vs All-on-4: Which Stays Fixed?

URL: https://www.renewimplants.ca/blog/snap-on-dentures-vs-all-on-4
Published: 2026-10-14
Updated: 2026-10-14
Query: snap-on dentures vs all-on-4

Snap-on dentures vs All-on-4 comes down to whether the teeth come out. A snap-on denture clips on and off. All-on-4 is a fixed full arch.

Short answer:

A snap-on denture comes out. All-on-4 stays fixed. This clinic describes a snap-on denture as a removable denture that clips onto two or four implants, and All-on-4 as a full arch fixed to four implants. The published All-on-4 concept is a fixed provisional prosthesis, and the evidence review behind it says the research is limited.

Key takeaways:

- A snap-on denture is removable. This clinic describes it clipping onto two or four implants.
- All-on-4, as this clinic describes it, is a fixed full arch on four implants.
- The published concept uses two straight and two angled implants and a provisional fixed prosthesis.
- A fixed bridge is not a removable denture, so the denturist's statutory scope is not the surgery.

Questions:

Q: Do snap-on dentures come out?
A: Yes. Renew's denture-alternative page describes a snap-on denture, also called an overdenture, as a denture that clips onto two or four implants and can be removed for cleaning.

Q: Does All-on-4 come out?
A: No. Renew's All-on-4 page describes a full arch fixed to four implants, unlike removable dentures. A 2017 review describes the published concept as a provisional fixed prosthesis on four implants.

Q: Is a snap-on denture the same as an implant-supported denture under the Canadian Dental Care Plan?
A: This comparison does not settle the plan. Read the article on the Canadian Dental Care Plan before you treat a snap-on denture as a covered denture.

Sources:

- Denture alternative — snap-on dentures (Renew Implant Centre): https://www.renewimplants.ca/services/denture-alternative
- All-on-4 dental implants (Renew Implant Centre): https://www.renewimplants.ca/services/all-on-4-dental-implants
- The all-on-four treatment concept: Systematic review (Journal of Clinical and Experimental Dentistry): https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5347302/
- Denturism Act, 1991, sections 3 and 4 (Government of Ontario): https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/91d25

## All-on-4 Recovery: What the First Weeks Feel Like

URL: https://www.renewimplants.ca/blog/all-on-4-recovery-first-weeks
Published: 2026-10-14
Updated: 2026-10-14
Query: all-on-4 recovery timeline

All-on-4 recovery timeline is not one calendar. A mandibular study attached a temporary bridge within two hours. It does not script your first weeks.

Short answer:

There is no single All-on-4 recovery calendar in the studies this page can cite. In one mandibular series, a provisional fixed acrylic bridge was attached within two hours of placing four implants. That paper does not describe your first weeks of swelling, diet, or time off work. If a mouth that has already been treated does not feel right, call the clinic.

Key takeaways:

- A 2003 mandibular series attached a provisional acrylic bridge within two hours. That timing belongs to that protocol.
- Published papers do not give a personal day-by-day pain, swelling, or diet calendar.
- Ordinary soreness is not the same as peri-implant disease.
- If something feels wrong after treatment, call the clinic. The quiz is for planning, not for a problem in progress.

Questions:

Q: Will I leave with teeth the same day?
A: In the 2003 Maló mandibular series, a provisional fixed acrylic prosthesis was attached within two hours. That is what that study did. It is not a schedule this page can assign to every person.

Q: How long will swelling and soreness last?
A: The studies cited here do not publish a personal day-by-day pain or swelling calendar, a time off work, or a diet schedule. Ask the clinic for the instructions that match your surgery.

Q: When is discomfort a reason to call?
A: Peri-implant disease is a clinical diagnosis: bleeding on probing, swelling, suppuration, deeper pockets or recession, and radiographic bone loss. Those signs are not the same as ordinary post-operative soreness. If a treated implant does not feel right, call the clinic.

Sources:

- "All-on-Four" immediate-function concept with Brånemark System implants for completely edentulous mandibles: a retrospective clinical study (Clinical Implant Dentistry and Related Research): https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12691645/
- Peri-implant diseases and conditions: Consensus report of workgroup 4 of the 2017 World Workshop (Journal of Clinical Periodontology): https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29926491/

## How Long Do All-on-4 Dental Implants Last?

URL: https://www.renewimplants.ca/blog/how-long-do-all-on-4-implants-last
Published: 2026-10-14
Updated: 2026-10-14
Query: how long do all-on-4 implants last

How long do All-on-4 implants last? One mandibular series reported 93% implant survival over 10 to 18 years, with almost a third of patients lost to follow-up.

Short answer:

In one mandibular All-on-4 series followed for 10 to 18 years, 93% of implants and 98.8% of the fixed prostheses were still counted as surviving. Almost one in three patients was lost to follow-up, so the percentage is not a personal forecast and it is not an upper-jaw result.

Key takeaways:

- In one mandibular series followed 10 to 18 years, cumulative prosthetic survival was 98.8% and implant survival was 93%.
- 149 of 471 patients, 31.6%, were lost to follow-up. Read the 93% next to that.
- Mean marginal bone loss was 1.72 mm at 10 years and 2.32 mm at 15 years.
- A separate review put mean implant survival between 94% and 98% at 72 to 132 months, and asked for larger trials.

Questions:

Q: How long did All-on-4 implants last in the longest cited study?
A: Maló and colleagues followed 471 mandibular All-on-4 patients for 10 to 18 years. Cumulative prosthetic survival was 98.8%. Cumulative implant survival was 93% and implant success was 91.7%. Almost a third of patients were lost to follow-up.

Q: Does 93% apply to me?
A: No. It is one group's retrospective series of lower jaws, with immediate function. It is not a personal prediction, and it is not an upper-jaw figure.

Q: What complications showed up over those years?
A: In that series, biological complications were 11.8% at implant level and mechanical complications were 36.7%. Previous biological complications were associated with later implant failure.

Sources:

- The All-on-4 treatment concept for the rehabilitation of the completely edentulous mandible: a longitudinal study with 10 to 18 years of follow-up (Clinical Implant Dentistry and Related Research): https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30924309/
- Survival rates of axial and tilted implants in the rehabilitation of edentulous jaws using the All-on-four concept: a systematic review (Journal of Indian Prosthodontic Society): https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33835063/

## Sedation for Dental Implant Surgery: What Are the Options?

URL: https://www.renewimplants.ca/blog/sedation-for-dental-implant-surgery
Published: 2026-10-14
Updated: 2026-10-14
Query: sedation for dental implant surgery

Sedation for dental implant surgery ranges from one oral sedative to general anaesthesia. Ontario dentists need current authorization for every level.

Short answer:

Ontario defines sedation from a single oral sedative or nitrous oxide up to general anaesthesia, and a dentist needs current authorization for every level. A facility permit is required once care goes beyond minimal sedation. Renew's own page lists oral sedation, IV sedation, and general anaesthesia, and says you need a ride home. Ask which authorization applies to your visit.

Key takeaways:

- In Ontario, a dentist needs current authorization for any level of sedation, including minimal.
- Minimal sedation is nitrous oxide with oxygen, or a single oral sedative. Deeper levels are defined separately.
- A facility permit is required for oral moderate sedation, parenteral sedation, deep sedation, and general anaesthesia.
- This clinic's sedation page lists oral sedation, IV sedation, and general anaesthesia, and says you need a ride home.

Questions:

Q: What sedation levels does the Royal College of Dental Surgeons of Ontario name?
A: Minimal sedation is nitrous oxide and oxygen, or a single oral sedative. Oral moderate, parenteral moderate, deep sedation, and general anaesthesia are separate levels. Parenteral routes include intravenous, intramuscular, subcutaneous, submucosal, and intranasal.

Q: Does every level need a facility permit?
A: No. The College says minimal sedation alone does not require a facility permit. Facilities providing oral moderate sedation, parenteral sedation, deep sedation, or general anaesthesia need a facility permit. Dentists still need current authorization for any level, including minimal.

Q: What does this clinic say it offers?
A: The sedation dentistry page describes oral sedation, IV sedation, and general anaesthesia, and says you will need someone to drive you home. Which option is available for a visit depends on the authorization the dentist and the facility hold. Ask that at the consultation.

Sources:

- Sedation and anesthesia permits (Royal College of Dental Surgeons of Ontario): https://www.rcdso.org/en-ca/permits-and-renewals/sedation-and-anesthesia
- Authorization to administer sedation and general anesthesia (Royal College of Dental Surgeons of Ontario): https://www.rcdso.org/permits-and-renewals/sedation-and-anesthesia/authorization-to-administer-sedation-and-general-anesthesia
- Sedation dentistry (Renew Implant Centre): https://www.renewimplants.ca/services/sedation-dentistry

## Can You Get Dental Implants If You Have Diabetes or Smoke?

URL: https://www.renewimplants.ca/blog/dental-implants-with-diabetes-or-smoking
Published: 2026-10-14
Updated: 2026-10-14
Query: dental implants with diabetes or smoking

Dental implants with diabetes or smoking show higher pooled failure rates in meta-analyses. Those percentages are not a personal forecast.

Short answer:

Smoking and diabetes are associated with higher pooled implant-failure rates. They are not a personal yes or no. A 2015 meta-analysis found failure in 6.35% of implants placed in smokers and 3.18% in non-smokers. A 2022 meta-analysis found higher odds of failure in people with diabetes. Both papers pool other people's studies. Neither one predicts your result.

Key takeaways:

- A 2015 meta-analysis found implant failure in 6.35% of implants in smokers and 3.18% in non-smokers.
- The same authors report a failure risk ratio of 2.23 and tell readers to interpret it cautiously.
- A 2022 meta-analysis found an odds ratio of 1.777 for failure in people with diabetes, which the authors describe as a 77.7% higher risk.
- Neither paper is a personal prognosis. Diabetes care and smoking are medical facts to bring to the consultation.

Questions:

Q: Does smoking mean a dental implant will fail?
A: No. In a 2015 meta-analysis, 6.35% of implants in smokers failed and 3.18% of implants in non-smokers failed. The risk ratio was 2.23. The authors say uncontrolled confounding means the result should be read with caution. It is not a personal failure rate.

Q: Does diabetes rule out implants?
A: Not as a blanket rule. A 2022 meta-analysis of 89 publications found a higher pooled failure risk in people with diabetes (odds ratio 1.777), which the authors describe as 77.7% higher than in people without diabetes. The difference was significant in the upper jaw and not in the lower jaw. It is not a forecast for one person.

Q: Should I tell the clinic?
A: Yes. Bring your diabetes care and whether you smoke to the consultation. The quiz does not replace that conversation or your physician.

Sources:

- Smoking and dental implants: a systematic review and meta-analysis (Journal of Dentistry): https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25778741/
- Diabetes mellitus and dental implants: a systematic review and meta-analysis (Materials): https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35591561/

## Denturist vs Dentist: Who Makes Your Implant Teeth?

URL: https://www.renewimplants.ca/blog/denturist-vs-dentist-for-implant-teeth
Published: 2026-10-14
Updated: 2026-10-14
Query: denturist vs dentist for dental implants

Denturist vs dentist for dental implants is a scope question in Ontario. A denturist fits removable dentures. An implant surgeon places the implants.

Short answer:

In Ontario, a denturist makes and fits removable dentures. A denturist does not place the implants. The Denturism Act is about removable dentures. A fixed All-on-4 bridge is a different appliance. At Renew, the implant surgeon places the implants, Tom Szarski, DD, is the denturist, and the on-site lab builds the teeth.

Key takeaways:

- Ontario's Denturism Act defines the work as removable dentures: assessing arches, and designing, making, repairing, and fitting them.
- A fixed All-on-4 bridge is not a removable denture.
- The College of Denturists of Ontario describes implant-supported denture fabrication inside that removable scope.
- At this clinic the implant surgeon places the implants. Tom Szarski, DD, is the denturist. The on-site lab builds the teeth.

Questions:

Q: Can a denturist place dental implants in Ontario?
A: The Denturism Act defines the practice as assessment of arches missing some or all teeth, and the design, construction, repair, alteration, ordering, and fitting of removable dentures. Placing an implant into the jaw is not that definition.

Q: Who makes a snap-on denture?
A: A snap-on denture is still a removable denture that clips onto implants. Removable denture work is the denturist's statutory scope. The implants themselves are placed by the implant surgeon.

Q: Who makes a fixed All-on-4 bridge?
A: A fixed bridge does not come out, so it is not the removable denture named in the Denturism Act. At Renew the implant surgeon places the implants and the on-site lab builds the teeth with the denturist.

Sources:

- Denturism Act, 1991 (Government of Ontario): https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/91d25
- Scope of practice (College of Denturists of Ontario): https://denturists-cdo.com/What-Does-a-Denturist-Do/Scope-of-Practice.aspx
- Meet your dentist (Renew Implant Centre): https://www.renewimplants.ca/meet-your-dentist

## Dental Implant Not Feeling Right: What to Do Next

URL: https://www.renewimplants.ca/blog/dental-implant-not-feeling-right
Published: 2026-10-14
Updated: 2026-10-14
Query: signs of dental implant failure

Signs of dental implant failure need a clinician and radiographs. Bleeding, pus, deeper pockets, and bone loss are published disease signs.

Short answer:

If a dental implant does not feel right, call the clinic that treated you. Do not wait on a quiz. Published signs of peri-implant disease include bleeding on probing, swelling, pus, deeper pockets or recession, and bone loss on a radiograph. A clinician makes that diagnosis. Ordinary soreness after surgery is a different conversation.

Key takeaways:

- Peri-implant health means no redness, no bleeding on probing, no swelling, and no pus.
- Peri-implantitis adds progressive bone loss to inflammation. A clinician and a radiograph make that call.
- A sore mouth after surgery is not the same list. Do not self-diagnose failure from a feeling.
- If you already have an implant that does not feel right, call the clinic. The quiz does not examine you.

Questions:

Q: What are published signs of peri-implant disease?
A: The 2017 World Workshop says peri-implant mucositis shows bleeding on gentle probing, and may show redness, swelling, or pus. Peri-implantitis adds progressive loss of supporting bone, with bleeding or pus, deeper pockets or recession, and bone loss on a radiograph.

Q: Can I tell at home that an implant has failed?
A: No. Those signs are diagnosed by a clinician with probing and radiographs. A feeling that something is loose or sore is a reason to call, not a diagnosis you can finish yourself.

Q: Who should I call?
A: If Renew treated you, call 613-841-6111 or use the contact page. If another clinic treated you, call that clinic. The implant candidate quiz is for people planning treatment, not for someone who already has a problem.

Sources:

- Peri-implant diseases and conditions: Consensus report of workgroup 4 of the 2017 World Workshop (Journal of Clinical Periodontology): https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29926491/
- Contact Renew Implant Centre (Renew Implant Centre): https://www.renewimplants.ca/contact-us

## All-on-4 vs All-on-6: What the Reviews Compared

URL: https://www.renewimplants.ca/blog/all-on-4-vs-all-on-6
Published: 2026-10-14
Updated: 2026-10-14
Query: all-on-4 vs all-on-6

All-on-4 vs all-on-6: a maxillary review found no significant survival gap, and more bone loss with four implants than with six.

Short answer:

All-on-4 vs all-on-6 compares how many implants hold a fixed full-arch bridge. A maxillary review found no significant survival difference, and significantly more bone loss with four implants. A 2026 pool of the named concepts also showed high survival for both, with wide heterogeneity. Neither paper chooses the number for your jaw.

Key takeaways:

- A 2024 review of maxillary fixed dentures found no significant survival difference between four and six implants.
- That same review found more marginal bone loss with four implants (1.02 mm) than with six (0.46 mm).
- A 2026 pooled review reported high survival for both All-on-4 and All-on-6, with high heterogeneity and one direct randomized trial.
- The implant count at this clinic comes from the 3D scan, bone, and the plan for that jaw.

Questions:

Q: Is All-on-6 safer than All-on-4?
A: Sharaf and colleagues found no significant survival difference between four and six implants in maxillary fixed dentures, and they did find more bone loss with four. Shao and colleagues reported high pooled survival for both named concepts, with high heterogeneity and only one randomized trial that compared them directly.

Q: Do those percentages tell me how many implants I need?
A: No. They pool other people's jaws. Sharaf 2024 is mostly maxillary fixed dentures. Shao 2026 mixed studies and had only one randomized trial that compared the two concepts directly. Your count depends on bone, the jaw, and the prosthesis.

Q: Can the upper jaw use more than four implants?
A: Yes. This clinic's upper-jaw page says some people are candidates for All-on-4 and others may benefit from six or more implants, depending on bone density and anatomy. A removable snap-on denture is a separate option.

Sources:

- Outcomes that may affect implant and prosthesis survival and complications in maxillary fixed prosthesis supported by four or six implants: A systematic review and meta-analysis (Heliyon): https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38317918/
- All-on-4 and All-on-6 implant concepts in edentulous patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis (International Journal of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery): https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijom.2026.04.002
- Upper jaw implants (Renew Implant Centre): https://www.renewimplants.ca/services/upper-jaw-implants

## What Is All-on-4? Four Implants and Fixed Teeth

URL: https://www.renewimplants.ca/blog/what-is-all-on-4
Published: 2026-10-14
Updated: 2026-10-14
Query: what is all-on-4

What is All-on-4? The 2003 series used four immediately loaded lower implants and a fixed acrylic bridge delivered within two hours of surgery.

Short answer:

What is All-on-4? In the 2003 paper, it is four lower-jaw implants loaded the same day with a fixed acrylic bridge. The back implants were tilted. The bridge in that series held at least 10 teeth and was made so the later version could reach about 12, with a cantilever of about one molar.

Key takeaways:

- The 2003 paper reported 44 lower jaws, 176 immediately loaded implants, and an acrylic bridge delivered within two hours.
- The back implants were tilted so the bridge could reach about 12 teeth with a short cantilever.
- Prosthesis survival in that series was 100%. Implant survival was 96.7% and 98.2% in the two groups.
- All-on-4 is one full-arch technique. Six implants, a snap-on denture, and single implants are other plans.

Questions:

Q: What is All-on-4 in the original paper?
A: Maló, Rangert, and Nobre described four implants in the lower jaw, in front of the nerve openings, loaded the same day with a fixed acrylic bridge. The series ran from April 1998 to June 2002 in a private clinic in Lisbon: 44 patients and 176 immediately loaded implants.

Q: Does All-on-4 mean any full set of implant teeth?
A: No. It is a specific four-implant immediate-function concept. A full arch can also be built on six or more implants, and a snap-on denture is removable. Those are different plans.

Q: Did everyone in that first series get extra rescue implants?
A: No. Twenty-four of the first 30 patients had 62 extra implants that were kept out of the temporary bridge. The authors later stopped placing them. The last third of the patients received only the four immediately loaded implants.

Sources:

- "All-on-Four" immediate-function concept with Branemark System implants for completely edentulous mandibles: a retrospective clinical study (Clinical Implant Dentistry and Related Research): https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12691645/
- All-on-4 dental implants (Renew Implant Centre): https://www.renewimplants.ca/services/all-on-4-dental-implants

## Temporary Teeth After All-on-4 Are Not the Final Set

URL: https://www.renewimplants.ca/blog/temporary-teeth-after-all-on-4
Published: 2026-10-14
Updated: 2026-10-14
Query: temporary teeth after all-on-4

Temporary teeth after All-on-4 were acrylic in the original series, and nine of the early bridges had a repairable fracture before the acrylic was thickened.

Short answer:

Temporary teeth after All-on-4, in the original series, were an acrylic bridge reinforced with a metal strip and delivered within two hours. Nine of the early ones fractured and were repaired. This clinic's page uses the same idea: teeth on the day of surgery, and a later bridge once the implants have integrated.

Key takeaways:

- The 2003 series delivered a metal-reinforced acrylic bridge within two hours of lower-jaw surgery.
- Nine of those early acrylic bridges, 30% of the development group, had a repairable fracture.
- After the acrylic was made thicker, the routine group in that series had no fractures during the study.
- A 2014 review named fracture of the all-acrylic bridge as the main prosthetic complication.

Questions:

Q: Are the teeth you leave with on surgery day the final bridge?
A: At this clinic, no. The All-on-4 page says most people receive implants and temporary teeth in one visit, and that the permanent bridge is placed a few months later. The 2003 series also started with acrylic, then made a different prosthesis for its first 30 patients.

Q: Why did the early acrylic bridges break?
A: Maló and colleagues reported repairable fractures in nine of the development-group acrylic prostheses, 30%. They then thickened the acrylic and cured it under higher pressure. The routine group had no fractures during the study. A 2014 review still names all-acrylic fracture as the main prosthetic complication of the concept.

Q: Did a fracture mean the implants had failed?
A: In the 2003 series, prosthesis survival was 100% even when an acrylic bridge needed repair. Implant losses were counted separately. A repairable fracture of the plastic teeth is a prosthetic event.

Sources:

- "All-on-Four" immediate-function concept with Branemark System implants for completely edentulous mandibles: a retrospective clinical study (Clinical Implant Dentistry and Related Research): https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12691645/
- The all-on-four treatment concept: a systematic review (Clinical Implant Dentistry and Related Research): https://doi.org/10.1111/cid.12068
- All-on-4 dental implants (Renew Implant Centre): https://www.renewimplants.ca/services/all-on-4-dental-implants

## When Do You Get the Final Teeth After All-on-4?

URL: https://www.renewimplants.ca/blog/when-do-you-get-final-teeth-after-all-on-4
Published: 2026-10-14
Updated: 2026-10-14
Query: when do you get final teeth after all-on-4

When do you get final teeth after All-on-4? One 2003 group waited 4 to 6 months. This clinic says a few months, with temporary teeth on day one.

Short answer:

When do you get final teeth after All-on-4? In the first published series, one group received a final prosthesis 4 to 6 months after surgery, and the other group mostly kept the reinforced acrylic. This clinic describes the later bridge as arriving in a few months, with temporary teeth already in place on the day of surgery.

Key takeaways:

- In the 2003 development group, final prostheses were made 4 to 6 months after surgery.
- The routine group in that paper mostly kept the reinforced acrylic, except two people who received titanium frameworks after 12 months.
- This clinic's All-on-4 page says the permanent bridge comes a few months later, and that people leave with temporary teeth the same day.
- A single month on a webpage would collapse two different protocols into one date.

Questions:

Q: When do you get the final teeth after All-on-4?
A: This clinic's All-on-4 page says the permanent bridge is placed within a few months, after the implants integrate, and that most people already have temporary teeth from the surgery visit. The 2003 paper used 4 to 6 months for one subgroup and a different schedule for the other.

Q: Did the original study give everyone a new bridge at 4 to 6 months?
A: No. That interval was for the development group of 30 patients. Their first seven finals were cast metal, and the other 23 were milled titanium. The routine group mostly continued with the reinforced acrylic. Two of those patients received titanium frameworks after 12 months.

Q: Are you without teeth while you wait?
A: The clinic page says you leave with teeth on day one. The wait it describes is the wait for the later bridge, not a wait with an empty jaw. What those first teeth were made of, and why some early acrylic ones fractured, is a separate question.

Sources:

- "All-on-Four" immediate-function concept with Branemark System implants for completely edentulous mandibles: a retrospective clinical study (Clinical Implant Dentistry and Related Research): https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12691645/
- All-on-4 dental implants (Renew Implant Centre): https://www.renewimplants.ca/services/all-on-4-dental-implants

## What the On-Site Lab Changes for All-on-4 Teeth

Updated: 2026-10-14
Query: on-site dental lab for all-on-4

An on-site dental lab for All-on-4 means the teeth are designed in this building. The studies do not show that the address changes implant survival.

Short answer:

An on-site dental lab for All-on-4, at this clinic, means the restoration is designed and made in the Orléans building rather than sent out. The published All-on-4 series describe what the prosthesis was made of. They do not show that keeping the lab on site changes how long the implants survive.

Key takeaways:

- The clinic says the sister lab in Orléans mills and prints the restorations, with no outsourcing.
- Named equipment on the team page: a PM7 mill, Asiga Professional Series printers, and 3Shape scanners, run by registered dental technicians.
- The 2003 series built a reinforced acrylic bridge the same day, then metal or milled titanium for one group of patients.
- Those papers do not compare an in-house lab with a lab in another building.

Questions:

Q: What is in the on-site lab?
A: The team page says the sister clinic, Orléans Denture Clinic, runs a full on-site lab staffed by registered dental technicians. The equipment named there is a PM7 milling machine, Asiga Professional Series printers, and 3Shape scanners, on a digital workflow, with no outsourcing.

Q: Does an on-site lab raise implant survival?
A: The All-on-4 studies cited here do not make that comparison. They describe the prosthesis: acrylic on the day of surgery in the 2003 series, then cast metal or milled titanium for one group. Survival in those papers is about implants and bridges, not about which building housed the lab.

Q: Who designs the teeth if the surgeon places the implants?
A: Tom Szarski, DD, is the denturist. He designs and fits the teeth. The implant surgeon places the implants. The lab technicians fabricate the restoration. Scope for the denturist, as distinct from the dentist who places implants, is explained in a separate article.

## Dental Implants vs a Bridge When Several Teeth Fail

URL: https://www.renewimplants.ca/blog/dental-implants-vs-bridge
Published: 2026-10-14
Updated: 2026-10-14
Query: dental implants vs bridge

Dental implants vs bridge, in a Canadian journal, meant one missing tooth: a three-unit bridge prepares the neighbours, and an implant leaves them alone.

Short answer:

Dental implants vs bridge, in the Canadian journal article that takes the question seriously, is a single-tooth choice. A three-unit bridge prepares the teeth next door. An implant is meant to leave those teeth alone. A jaw full of failing teeth is a different problem from that one gap.

Key takeaways:

- Hebel, Gajjar, and Hofstede wrote about replacing one tooth, in the Journal of the Canadian Dental Association in 2000.
- A conventional three-unit bridge reduces the neighbouring teeth. The authors said that raises the chance of root-canal treatment and root decay when those teeth were sound or lightly filled.
- They also wrote that cement washout can lead to tooth loss, and that failure of one part can take an abutment tooth with it.
- A full arch of failing teeth is a different comparison from that single gap.

Questions:

Q: What is the difference between a dental implant and a bridge for one missing tooth?
A: Hebel, Gajjar, and Hofstede, in the Journal of the Canadian Dental Association, said a conventional three-unit bridge requires reduction of the teeth on either side. An implant replaces the missing tooth without preparing those neighbours. They were writing about a single gap.

Q: Do the neighbouring teeth have to be cut down for a bridge?
A: For the conventional three-unit bridge they describe, yes. They wrote that the reduction increases the incidence of endodontic treatment and root decay, and that sound teeth or teeth with small fillings would be damaged by that preparation. Teeth that already have large restorations, they said, may benefit from being used as abutments.

Q: Does that article decide a full mouth of failing teeth?
A: No. It is a single-tooth paper. When many teeth are failing, the comparison is a full-arch plan or a denture plan, not a three-unit bridge repeated across the jaw. Those options are separate articles.

Sources:

- Single-tooth replacement: bridge vs. implant-supported restoration (Journal of the Canadian Dental Association): https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11040527/

## Denture Adhesive vs Teeth That Stay In

URL: https://www.renewimplants.ca/blog/denture-adhesive-vs-implants
Published: 2026-10-14
Updated: 2026-10-14
Query: denture adhesive vs implants

Denture adhesive vs implants: a 2002 consensus called widespread adhesive a sign that many dentures fall short, especially the lower one.

Short answer:

Denture adhesive vs implants, in the McGill consensus, starts with a blunt observation: widespread adhesive is one sign that conventional dentures are inadequate for many people. The treatment they put first for a lower jaw with no teeth was a two-implant overdenture. That is a removable denture that clips on. It is not All-on-4.

Key takeaways:

- The McGill consensus said widespread denture adhesive is one sign that conventional dentures are inadequate for many wearers.
- The alternative they named was a mandibular two-implant overdenture, tested against new conventional dentures for 6 months to 9 years.
- That overdenture still comes out. It clips on with a bar, ball, or magnet. It is not a fixed All-on-4 bridge.
- People in the trials found the two-implant denture more stable, easier for chewing and speech, and more comfortable.

Questions:

Q: Does denture adhesive mean the denture is failing?
A: The McGill consensus treated widespread adhesive use as one indication that conventional dentures are inadequate for many wearers. It is a sign across a population, not a diagnosis of one tube in one bathroom. The statement focused on the lower denture.

Q: What did the consensus recommend instead?
A: A two-implant overdenture on the lower jaw, as the first-choice treatment for an edentulous mandible. Trials of 6 months to 9 years, using bar, ball, or magnet attachments, found people more satisfied than with new conventional dentures. That denture is still removable.

Q: Is that the same thing as All-on-4?
A: No. All-on-4 is a fixed bridge on four implants. The McGill statement is about two implants and a denture that clips on and comes out. A fixed full arch is a third option, described in the snap-on comparison.

Sources:

- The McGill consensus statement on overdentures. Mandibular two-implant overdentures as first choice standard of care for edentulous patients (Gerodontology): https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12164236/

## Upper Denture vs Upper All-on-4: What Changes

URL: https://www.renewimplants.ca/blog/upper-denture-vs-all-on-4
Published: 2026-10-14
Updated: 2026-10-14
Query: upper denture vs all-on-4

Upper denture vs All-on-4: the McGill statement said people usually manage an upper denture. A fixed upper arch is a separate plan.

Short answer:

Upper denture vs All-on-4 is not the comparison the McGill consensus was built to settle. That statement said people usually manage an upper denture, and that the mobile one is the lower denture. A fixed upper arch is a different prosthesis from both the upper plate and the two-implant lower overdenture they recommended.

Key takeaways:

- The McGill consensus said complete-denture wearers are usually able to wear an upper denture without problems.
- The struggle they described was the lower denture, because it is too mobile.
- A fixed upper All-on-4 bridge is not the two-implant lower overdenture that statement recommended.
- This clinic's upper-jaw page allows for four implants, six or more, or a removable snap-on, depending on the jaw.

Questions:

Q: Is an upper denture usually the difficult one?
A: The McGill consensus said the opposite of that folk rule. Complete denture wearers are usually able to wear an upper denture without problems. Many struggle to eat with the complete lower denture because it is too mobile.

Q: What is upper All-on-4, if the upper denture often works?
A: All-on-4 is a fixed bridge on four implants. It is not a removable upper plate, and it is not the two-implant lower overdenture from the consensus. People still choose it when they want the upper teeth fixed, or when the upper denture is the part that fails for them. The consensus did not study that choice.

Q: Does every upper jaw get exactly four implants?
A: No. This clinic's upper-jaw page says some people are candidates for All-on-4 and others may benefit from six or more implants, depending on bone density and anatomy. A snap-on overdenture is the removable implant option on that page.

Sources:

- The McGill consensus statement on overdentures. Mandibular two-implant overdentures as first choice standard of care for edentulous patients (Gerodontology): https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12164236/
- Upper jaw implants (Renew Implant Centre): https://www.renewimplants.ca/services/upper-jaw-implants

## Lower Denture vs Lower Implants: What the Evidence Says

URL: https://www.renewimplants.ca/blog/lower-denture-vs-implants
Published: 2026-10-14
Updated: 2026-10-14
Query: lower denture vs implants

Lower denture vs implants: the McGill consensus recommended two implants and a removable overdenture, a different plan from a fixed All-on-4 bridge.

Short answer:

Lower denture vs implants, in the McGill consensus, comes out as a two-implant overdenture. People usually cope with the upper denture. Many cannot eat well with the lower one because it moves. The statement's first choice for that lower jaw is a removable denture clipped to two implants, which is a different treatment from All-on-4.

Key takeaways:

- Many complete-denture wearers struggle to eat with the lower denture because it is too mobile.
- The McGill consensus recommended a two-implant mandibular overdenture as the first choice for an edentulous lower jaw.
- Trials from 6 months to 9 years found that denture more stable, more comfortable, and easier for chewing and speech than a new conventional denture.
- Two implants and a clip-in denture are not four implants and a fixed All-on-4 bridge.

Questions:

Q: Why does a lower denture move more than an upper one?
A: The McGill consensus said complete denture wearers are usually able to wear an upper denture without problems, but many struggle to eat with the complete lower denture because it is too mobile. Conventional dentures depend on the residual ridge and the mucosa, and the statement says the mandibular one is the harder adaptation.

Q: How many implants did the consensus recommend?
A: Two, in the lower jaw, holding a removable overdenture with a bar, ball, or magnet. That was their first-choice treatment for an edentulous mandible. It is not a fixed bridge and it is not All-on-4.

Q: What improved in the trials?
A: Across randomized and non-randomized trials lasting 6 months to 9 years, people were significantly more satisfied with the two-implant overdenture than with a new conventional denture. They found it more stable, easier for chewing, more comfortable, and easier for speech. Quality-of-life ratings were higher when that lower overdenture opposed a conventional upper denture.

Sources:

- The McGill consensus statement on overdentures. Mandibular two-implant overdentures as first choice standard of care for edentulous patients (Gerodontology): https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12164236/
- Lower jaw implants (Renew Implant Centre): https://www.renewimplants.ca/services/lower-jaw-implants
